question: A university course administrator must confirm that a Claude-drafted section of the student handbook matches the university's published regulations. In which order should these steps be taken?
options: A) Find each of those statements in the published regulations; identify the statements in the section that assert a regulation; correct any statement the regulations do not support; record which version of the regulations was used.

B) Identify the statements in the section that assert a regulation; find each of those statements in the published regulations; correct any statement the regulations do not support; record which version of the regulations was used.

C) Correct any statement the regulations do not support; identify the statements in the section that assert a regulation; find each of those statements in the published regulations; record which version of the regulations was used.

D) Identify the statements in the section that assert a regulation; correct any statement the regulations do not support; find each of those statements in the published regulations; record which version of the regulations was used.
correct_answers: B) Identify the statements in the section that assert a regulation; find each of those statements in the published regulations; correct any statement the regulations do not support; record which version of the regulations was used.
explanations: She would be looking statements up before deciding which statements matter, so the search has no defined scope and ordinary descriptive sentences get treated as regulatory claims.

Correct. Singling out the sentences that make a regulatory claim scopes the work; each of those is then traced to the published regulations, which is the authoritative source rather than the draft itself; corrections follow from what that comparison found; and recording the version used makes the check repeatable when the regulations change.
Editing comes first of all, before either the claims have been identified or the regulations opened, so the handbook is changed on no evidence at all.
Corrections are made before the regulations have been consulted, which means they rest on what she assumes the rules say. The lookup that should have driven the edits arrives after them.
